title: The ELI Scheme: BMS welcomes, but asks for quality jobs
author: Editorial Desk
summary: In July 2025 BMS welcomed the Employment Linked Incentive scheme and listed what it wants alongside it.
body:
*Photo: BMS statement on the ELI Scheme, July 2025*

On 1 July 2025 the Union Cabinet approved the **Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) Scheme**, which is meant to encourage employers to create new jobs and to help first-time workers join the formal workforce. The scheme had been announced in the Union Budget for 2024-25. The next day, 2 July 2025, BMS welcomed it in a press statement, while listing what it wants alongside it. This post sets out what the scheme provides, what BMS said, what others have worried about, and what a worker should look for.

## What the scheme provides

According to the Press Information Bureau, the ELI Scheme has an outlay of **Rs 99,446 crore** and aims to support the creation of more than **3.5 crore jobs** over two years. It covers jobs created between **1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027**. It has two parts.

**Part A, for first-time employees.** It covers first-time employees registered with the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), about 1.92 crore people. They receive one month's EPF wage, up to Rs 15,000, in two instalments. The first comes after six months of service, and the second after twelve months of service and the completion of a financial literacy programme. Employees with salaries up to Rs 1 lakh a month are eligible. Part of the incentive is kept in a savings deposit that the employee can withdraw later, and payment is made by direct benefit transfer through the Aadhaar Bridge Payment System.

**Part B, for employers.** Employers receive up to **Rs 3,000 per month for two years** for each additional employee who is kept on for at least six months, where the employee earns up to Rs 1 lakh a month. For manufacturing, the support extends to the third and fourth years. The amount depends on the employee's EPF wage: up to Rs 1,000 where the wage is up to Rs 10,000, Rs 2,000 where it is between Rs 10,000 and Rs 20,000, and up to Rs 3,000 above that. An employer must be registered with EPFO and must hire at least two additional employees if it has fewer than 50 staff, or five if it has 50 or more, and retain them for six months. The scheme is expected to cover about 2.60 crore additional jobs through this part.

## BMS's reaction

BMS issued its statement through its General Secretary and described the Cabinet decision as a historic step towards creating employment, praising the size of the outlay and the target. It also said that the number of jobs should not overshadow their quality, and it asked the Government for:

- **quality employment**, with incentives limited to employers who offer stable, secure and well-paid work,
- **worker protections**, including fair wages, health protection, provident fund, ESI and other statutory benefits, so that incentives do not lead to casualisation or contractualisation, and an assurance that short-term or contract hiring is not done only to claim the incentive,
- **priority for rural, micro and small-scale manufacturing and ancillary industries**, which are the largest job creators, and
- safeguards so that large corporations do not capture most of the benefit at the expense of smaller players.

BMS also said it would cooperate with the Government and with employers to implement the scheme effectively.

## The reasoning

BMS's approach is to support what helps workers and the nation, and to say clearly what needs attention. Its argument is that an incentive should be tied to the **quality** of employment and not just to the number of people on a payroll. A job that lasts six months and ends is a statistic, but a job with a wage, a record and a future is a livelihood.

The labour market gives reason to take this seriously. The Periodic Labour Force Survey for 2023-24 found that 58.4 per cent of workers were self-employed and only 21.7 per cent were regular wage or salaried employees. The India Employment Report 2024, by the ILO and the Institute for Human Development, noted that the share of regular employment had started to fall after 2018, and that youth make up almost 83 per cent of the unemployed. A scheme that moves first-time workers onto an EPFO register is therefore addressing a real gap, as long as the jobs themselves are decent.

## Concerns raised by others

Analysts and some unions have raised questions that are worth stating plainly:

- **Who administers it?** The scheme uses the EPFO, which holds workers' savings and which, in the view of some unions, was not set up to run a job-creation scheme. Some have asked for a dedicated agency. The concern reported is that workers' savings should not be diverted to subsidise employers.
- **Past experience.** Unions have pointed to earlier production-linked incentives, whose benefits they say went to large firms without much job creation.
- **Hiring for the incentive.** Firms may inflate hiring for a short period to capture the benefit. The six-month retention rule is intended to limit this.
- **Small firms.** Because employers must be registered with EPFO, unregistered units are excluded, and some experts have suggested that smaller units with fewer than 20 employees be brought in. MSMEs support livelihoods for over 12 crore people and contribute around 30 per cent of GDP, according to the Ministry of MSME's year-end review for 2025, so how they fare matters a great deal.
- **Verification.** Strong checks are needed to prevent false reporting of employment.

These are concerns and not findings. The scheme has only just begun, and its record will show what actually happens.

## What to look for

- How the scheme is **monitored**, and whether results are published.
- Whether first-time workers receive **appointment letters** and are registered under EPFO from the first day.
- Whether **small units** can claim the incentive without heavy paperwork.
- Whether new hires remain in employment after the incentive period ends.
- Whether the **financial literacy** requirement is simple to complete for workers in small towns.

## Closing

For the worker, the question is plain: does this job come with a wage, a record and a future? If the ELI Scheme answers yes for even a part of the 3.5 crore targeted, it will matter. If it counts jobs without checking their quality, it will fall short of what workers need. BMS's position, to welcome the step and to hold it to a standard, is the one that a union is expected to take.
